html:
The first record of tomatoes in Italy dates from 1548, when a basket of them was sent to the household of Cosimo de' Medici, Duke of Florence, in Tuscany. The plant came from the Americas, where it had been grown in Mexico long before the Spanish arrived, part of the Columbian Exchange.

At first Italians grew it more as a curiosity than as food. A botanist called the fruit pomi d'oro, golden apples, which is why Italians still say pomodoro. Many Europeans were wary of it, since it belongs to the same family as deadly nightshade.

It took well over a century to reach the cooking pot. The first printed Italian recipe for a tomato sauce appeared in Naples in the 1690s, described as "Spanish style", since Naples was then ruled by Spain. In the 1800s tomato sauce, pasta and pizza in Naples made the American fruit central to Italian food, and Italian migrants carried that food around the world.
